touches.text: Coding Ticket: what we usually mean.
TESTER MACHINE, CodeMother's (was the tester device, cairn/devices/tester/)
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.
gate: the == compare, in one place. A gate opens when every expected equals its actual. No oracle, ever.

A sieve's rule follows the ticket's kind (Akien, 2026-10-31: "for new/changed code tickets the rule is x, for fixit tickets the rule is y"). It is read off the ticket, so it stays deterministic, and 19.14.7 is left for what x and y do not cover.

x, new or changed code (code-seam): at BUILDME the named proof exists and its PROVES names the ticket, and it may be red, since a new proof is red before its build. At PROVED it is sealed green and hollow-measured.

y, fixit (bug): at BUILDME the ticket names the red it fixes (the proof), and that proof really is red on disk now; the named proof may be red, fixing it is the job. The fix may change the test case itself without a ruling: the proof's why names the ticket and says what it tests and why it changed, and names any tooth it removed. At PROVED it is sealed green and hollow-measured, as x.

A ticket cannot call itself a fixit to get y: y needs a real red on disk, which code checks. The harbor's proven-space rule (5.9) and the tester's rung 4 (11) each apply x or y by the ticket's kind; rung 4 no longer asks who answered.

open_questions.text: What keeps the after-failure check from being a lock pick: a reader other than the builder (a cold cheap model, as rehearsal), the finding recording both whys verbatim and which lost, a pass that dies with its one ticket, a per-sieve count of passes that reds the sieve past some number? Which of these, or what else?
